name: PCA major territory
summary: The posterior cerebral artery major territory is the occipital lobe, the inferomedial temporal lobe (parahippocampal and fusiform gyri, hippocampus), the splenium and, through the thalamoperforating, thalamogeniculate and posterior choroidal arteries, most of the thalamus and part of the midbrain. This level-2 map merges the occipital and temporal PCA cortical domains with the thalamic and midbrain perforator territories, and it is the territory infarcted in a P1 or P2 occlusion, most often embolic from the heart or the vertebrobasilar system. Its signature is a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, with memory loss, alexia, visual agnosia and thalamic sensory loss according to the extent, and bilateral infarction produces cortical blindness.

anatomy.location: Medial and inferior occipital lobe (calcarine cortex, cuneus, lingual gyrus), the occipital pole, the inferomedial temporal lobe (parahippocampal, fusiform and inferior temporal gyri, hippocampus), the splenium, and the deep territory of the thalamus (except the tuberothalamic part when the PComm supplies it), the subthalamus and the medial midbrain; bounded by the MCA territory laterally and the ACA territory at the parieto-occipital sulcus.

afferents.from: Posterior cerebral artery P1-P4 segments and perforators

efferents.to: Basal vein of Rosenthal and the great cerebral vein, transverse sinus

function: The territory contains the primary and association visual cortex, the ventral visual stream of object and face recognition, the medial temporal memory system, the splenial fibers that join the two visual cortices and the thalamic relays of sensation, arousal and memory, so its infarction produces visual, memory and sensory syndromes rather than weakness, unless the midbrain peduncle is involved. Leptomeningeal collaterals from the MCA spare the occipital pole (macular sparing) in many cases; the perforator territories have none. Embolic occlusion of the basilar tip involves both PCAs and the thalami at once.

bestView.label: PCA territory over the occipital and medial temporal lobes
PCA domain from the splenium to the occipital pole

imaging.normalAppearance: On the overlay the PCA domain covers the medial occipital and inferomedial temporal surfaces and the thalamus; the calcarine cortex and hippocampus are its core.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the medial occipital lobe with or without the medial temporal lobe and thalamus; homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing when the pole survives.
Bilateral PCA, thalamic and midbrain infarcts with cortical blindness, somnolence, vertical gaze palsy and amnesia.
Bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic edema in the PCA-MCA border region with visual symptoms; reversible, not infarction.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Calcarine cortex or optic radiation infarction

lesionEffects.deficit: Alexia without agraphia, visual agnosia (left), prosopagnosia (right)

lesionEffects.mechanism: Medial temporal and thalamic perforator infarction

lesionEffects.deficit: Cortical blindness with denial when bilateral

examination: Sensation on the contralateral body when the thalamus is involved
pearls: A stroke with a hemianopia and no weakness is a PCA stroke until the CT says otherwise
Macular sparing means the MCA fed the pole, not that the stroke was small
PCA infarcts are embolic more often than any other territory: look at the heart and the vertebral arteries
